In [[cryptography]], an '''all-or-nothing transform''' ('''AONT'''), also known as an '''all-or-nothing protocol''', is an [[Block cipher modes of operation|encryption mode]] which allows the data to be understood only if all of it is known. AONTs are not encryption, but frequently make use of symmetric ciphers and may be applied before encryption. In exact terms, "an AONT is an unkeyed, invertible, randomized transformation, with the property that it is hard to invert unless all of the output is known."<ref name=Boyko>{{cite book|last=Boyko|first=Victor |title=Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO' 99 |chapter=On the Security Properties of OAEP as an All-or-Nothing Transform |year=1999|doi=10.1007/3-540-48405-1_32|url=http://theory.lcs.mit.edu/~cis/cis-exposure.html|volume=1666|pages=503–518|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|isbn=978-3-540-66347-8}}</ref>

==Algorithms==
The original AONT, the ''package transform'', was described by [[Rivest|Ronald L. Rivest]] in his 1997 paper [http://theory.lcs.mit.edu/~cis/pubs/rivest/fusion.ps "All-Or-Nothing Encryption and The Package Transform"].<ref>{{cite book|last=Rivest|first=Ronald |title=Fast Software Encryption |chapter=All-or-nothing encryption and the package transform |year=1997|doi=10.1007/BFb0052348|url=http://theory.lcs.mit.edu/~cis/pubs/rivest/fusion.ps|volume=1267|pages=210–218|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|isbn=978-3-540-63247-4}}</ref> The transform that Rivest proposed involved preprocessing the [[plaintext]] by [[XOR]]ing each plaintext block with that block's index encrypted by a randomly chosen key, then appending one extra block computed by XORing that random key and the hashes of all the preprocessed blocks. The result of this preprocessing is called the ''pseudomessage'', and it serves as the input to the encryption algorithm. Undoing the package transform requires hashing every block of the pseudomessage except the last, XORing all the hashes with the last block to recover the random key, and then using the random key to convert each preprocessed block back into its original plaintext block. In this way, it's impossible to recover the original plaintext without first having access to every single block of the pseudomessage.

Although Rivest's paper only gave a detailed description of the package transform as it applies to [[Block cipher modes of operation|CBC]] mode, it can be implemented using a cipher in any [[Block cipher modes of operation|mode]]. Therefore, there are multiple variants: the package [[Block cipher modes of operation|ECB]] transform, package CBC transform, etc.

In 1999 Victor Boyko proposed another AONT, provably secure under the [[random oracle model]].<ref name=Boyko /> 

Apparently at about the same time, D. R. Stinson proposed a different implementation of AONT, without any cryptographic assumptions.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Stinson|first=D. R.|title=Something About All or Nothing (Transforms)|journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography|date=1 January 2001|volume=22|issue=2|pages=133–138|doi=10.1023/A:1008304703074|s2cid=10118200 }}</ref> This implementation is a linear transform, perhaps highlighting some security weakness of the original definition.

==Applications==
AONTs can be used to increase the strength of encryption without increasing the key size. This may be useful to, for example, secure secrets while complying with government [[Export of cryptography|cryptography export regulations]]. AONTs help prevent several attacks.

One of the ways AONTs improve the strength of encryption is by preventing attacks which reveal only part of the information from revealing anything, as the partial information is not enough to recover any of the original message.

Another application, suggested in the original papers is to reduce the cost of security: for example, a file can be processed by AONT, and then only a small portion of it can be encrypted (e.g., on a smart-card). AONT will assure that as a result the whole file is protected. It is important to use the stronger version of the transform (such as the one by Boyko above).

AONT may be combined with [[forward error correction]] to yield a computationally secure [[secret sharing]] scheme.<ref>{{cite conference |url=https://web.eecs.utk.edu/~plank/plank/papers/FAST-2011.pdf |title=AONT-RS: Blending Security and Performance in Dispersed Storage Systems |first=Jason |last=Resch |author2=Plank, James |date=February 15, 2011 |conference=Usenix FAST'11 |conference-url=https://www.usenix.org/events/fast11/ }}</ref>

Other uses of AONT can be found in [[optimal asymmetric encryption padding]] (OAEP).
